essays.title: If You're a Founder, Read This
essays.teaser: Everyone wants to be a founder. But what actually makes you one? Being a founder isn't registering a company, building a product in stealth, or becoming your own boss. I think the answer lies somewhere between ownership, agency and legacy: what you choose to build, why it has to be yours, and what you hope remains when you're gone.
essays.cadenceTeaser: What makes someone a founder beyond registering a company or starting a project? How I discovered founderhood.
essays.dek: Everyone wants to be a founder. But what actually makes you one?

body.text: Earlier this year, I picked up Founders at Work, by Y Combinator co-founder Jessica Livingston, and it sent me back to a question I didn’t know I was looking for an answer to: what does it mean to be a founder? How do you identify them? Is it by the work, the vision, the lifestyle or the legacy? Somewhere along the way, I not only realized what being a founder meant – at least to me – but why I had finally chosen to become one.

Being a founder really isn’t as simple as registering a company or becoming your own boss. Anyone who lives in a capitalist society can do that. The better question – I think – is the relationship you have with founderhood. Perhaps, I made this word up. But I genuinely believe it is as important of a force to examine as parenthood, adulthood, or neighborhood.

The moment you decide to be a founder, you’re immediately hit with the question of “why do you want to do this”? Out of everything you could’ve picked “why this?”. This essay is an exploration of this question.
Is it what you do?

Some people go through the motions of being a founder. They normally start by buying a domain, designing a logo or registering the company – to signal serious intention. These are outward facing motions that establish the legitimacy of what someone is doing. It is ownership in a sense, because you technically own these assets. However, you also begin to start owning the responsibility of putting these assets to work.

Moving into the ‘day-to-day’, founders may start introducing themselves as the brains behind the operations. The more serious ones will go through motions of planning, hiring, delegating to team members and interviewing users or approaching potential clients to secure new sales contracts. This is what I believe, separates a “real founder” from say, a “fake founder”. A real founder owns everything, from initial concept to business management.

A fake founder can have a shell of a company, the title to go with it and potentially an initial idea but hasn’t fully acted upon it themselves or has otherwise chosen to fully delegate the work to others. They can hire someone to interview those users, build the product or deck, or hire someone to procure the contracts on their behalf and increasingly they can delegate all of this to AI.

However, if AI can increasingly do the things we associate with founders – research the market, write the code, design the product, build the deck, run the outreach, what's left that only the founder can do?

Sometimes people talk about how founders are the ones who make the decisions, especially the tough ones at 1am or the ones that leave your feet up in the air. They are the ones doing the negotiation, managing stakeholders in high-stake rooms and moving the conversation forward. This indeed requires a certain level of judgement and intuition that AI can’t replace.

An AI agent may be able to schedule a coffee chat on your behalf, take meeting notes and predict what you may want to say in a follow-up email with better next steps you could’ve jotted down yourself, but the limits are often defined by organization capabilities and predictability. AI doesn’t come up with ideas or solutions, the founder does.

When faced with fast-changing scenarios or deciding the timing or tone of a particular response, an AI agent will act with far less bandwidth for a successful outcome. Arguably, the founder needs to be the pacesetter, based on where they think the company is heading. The decisions they make can’t be outsourced but need to be found from within themselves. Oftentimes, these decisions reflect a founder’s own personal values or their personal understanding of a company’s vision, mission or purpose.

If tasks can increasingly be delegated but judgment cannot, perhaps founderhood has less to do with doing than with owning the overall direction. In that case, does being a founder mean you’re the one who owns the vision?
Is it the vision?

Many times, founders are rabble-rousers coming from outside an industry. These are the ones that typically make it onto Forbes 30 under 30, which pre-selects based on the size and scale of the business, originality of the idea or future potential. PR-gimmick or not, it is an aspirational shorthand for people to announce, “they are doing something big”. Whatever people think, these founders have successfully sold the idea to a Forbes editor that “they have a vision” for the world, one that is distinct and has some real momentum behind it.

A lot of successful founders we hear about are referred to as “industry trailblazers”. We talk about them in a way where we assume, at least to a certain degree, they have an interest in making meaningful changes to a system. They often do so by achieving one of three things: i. creating a new cross-industry category, ii. applying a new model to an old problem, or iii. scaling something much faster than existing market incumbents.

Not all innovation is technological, sometimes innovation is operational. That said, I would argue that a founder’s interpretation of the world or the problem at hand, often contributes to better “operational execution”. Indeed, plenty of excellent founders win by executing unusually better than others in an existing market with better product, distribution, insights or simply better timing.

Being on an industry list doesn’t necessarily validate someone will succeed or fail, or create positive impact through their new venture (oftentimes, the contrary holds). However, the scale of it often matters, as they have successfully sold an idea or vision that has achieved external validation: from major customers, credible investors, respected partners. With industry adoption, awards and publications, a founder cements the validity of their vision and ingredients that will inevitably shape their legacy.

Many people have an idea, but not everyone can execute the idea successfully. Simply put, it is not easy to change industry norms overnight or capture market share from large industry players, therefore someone normally needs to be driven by their vision or purpose to become a founder, especially a start-up founder.
With vision, ownership becomes not mere ownership of the company, but of the outcome, and ultimately the mark you want to leave behind.

In most instances, I would argue founders are driven by positive outcomes. However, the size and scale of a founder’s ambition and where they want to contribute positive outcomes also has a few determining factors.
Is it the lifestyle?

A question I’ve been pondering for the past few months is what distinguishes a start-up founder from other kinds of founders — small business owners, content creators and lifestyle entrepreneurs, or people building on their family business. At first, I wondered whether it was the number of pivots, freshness of the idea, or simply the amount of uncertainty involved. But I think there’s a cleaner distinction: the shape of capital and ambition. There’s a difference between running a small café in your local neighbourhood and accounting practice for a roster of clients and starting a business that you think will disrupt an entire industry.

Each type of founder is building toward something slightly different. For instance, a small-business owner builds a company that provides livelihood and independence. A lifestyle entrepreneur builds a company partly to serve their lifestyle. Small businesses serve as an important part of local economies, and founders of small businesses often have an outsized impact on their local communities. Meanwhile, influencers could extend their reach from niche groups to global communities.

A family-business founder builds an institution intended to outlive them and remain under family or community stewardship. Meanwhile, a startup founder attempts to build an institution that can eventually become much bigger than them. They are not operating on a well-known playbook, and the control they have to give up almost becomes inevitable.

They may all be “founders”, and from the outside they can share the same founder vibe or aesthetic. But the underlying reality can be very different: what the business is designed to do, what capital it needs, what risks it takes and what the founder is ultimately trying to create.

rows: Usually personal capital, debt or retained earnings; capital supports the business.
Build something profitable, durable and independent.
Typically, low-capital and revenue-funded; the individual is often the core asset.
Maximize autonomy, income, audience and/or lifestyle.
Preserve, compound and pass on an institution to the next generation.
Often external, risk-seeking capital invested ahead of profitability, to help scale a vision.
Build something capable of nonlinear growth and outsized impact or value.

body.text: The important distinction isn’t that one form of ambition is inherently bigger or better. A family business can become a multibillion-dollar company; a creator can reach hundreds of millions of people. It is the shape of the ambition, the intended trajectory and the relationship to scale that differ. Start-ups are grease to the wheels of the real economy. The backbone of innovation. As such, they require different models of funding and risk tolerance.

Most people mistake startup founders for wanting control over people, but I think they simply want agency to shape what gets created. That is the other irony of it, the more successful a startup becomes, the more a founder will have to give up control. If the company is going to become larger than the founder, it cannot remain entirely theirs.
Is it the legacy?

What is worth separating is founder lifestyle from founder legacy. Lifestyle is the part a founder experiences directly, whereas legacy is what travels outward: from the company to the customers it changes, the jobs it creates, the markets it enters, the systems it alters and, eventually, what remains after the founder is no longer at the centre of it.

If lifestyle is what the founder gets to experience, legacy is what the company leaves behind. For a startup founder, that legacy is tied to a particular kind of ambition: trying to build something that can grow beyond the founder’s own time, relationships and direct control. That brings me back to the idea of “search” — not the search for a job, but the search for the biggest version of a problem you are willing to spend years solving.

Paul Graham has written about the idea of finding a project of your own. I like that framing because it makes founderhood feel less like a title and more like a commitment. The best founders I know are builders in the broadest sense – not just mechanical or molecular engineers or scientists, but designers, operators, hackers and architects of systems. They make something people want, then keep taking responsibility for what that thing becomes.
The deeper question is why some of us feel compelled to build something of our own in the first place.

I think this relates to why the founder’s relationship with the problem matters so much. Maybe what attracts founders is not control itself, but agency: the ability to bring something into existence that otherwise would not exist. The startup founder may be one of the more extreme expressions of that impulse, accepting an eventual loss of control in exchange for increasing the magnitude of what can be created for their customers, employees, investors, and, eventually, the institution itself.
In that sense, legacy is consequence: the part of what you built that continues to matter beyond your direct involvement.
On Ambitious Founders

Last year, I went to a talk by HBS professor Jeff Bussgang, where he makes the case for more founders in the Age of AI. In Experimentation Machine, Bussgang argues AI isn’t going to replace founders, but founders who use AI are going to replace founders who don’t. AI may change the founder’s toolkit, but it does not remove the need for someone to decide what is worth building, why it matters and the trade-offs during its building process.
Being a founder isn't a checklist of activities. It's a relationship to what you're building.

If there’s one thing I’ve learned this year, it’s that founderhood is a relationship a founder has with capital and ambition. This is often underpinned by one’s understanding of ownership, agency and legacy: what you choose to build, why it has to be yours, and what you hope remains when you're gone.

I spent my entire twenties in search of a dream job. It wasn't until the tail end of the decade that I realized the job didn't exist, and I had to create it for myself. I was looking for a role inside someone else’s system when, really, I wanted the agency to help shape the system itself. That’s the moment when I found founderhood.

If I’m honest, I am less motivated by the idea that I have one singular problem in the world that only I am meant to solve. I am more drawn to people who are already solving hard problems — and to helping them solve those problems better, faster and at a scale they could not reach on their own. I think I am motivated less by my own purpose than by other people’s: by being useful to what they are already trying to build. That, in itself, may be my purpose.

I decided that I didn’t want to be a founder of a boutique consultancy with <$5M ARR, I wanted to build a product that could change people’s relationship to founderhood. That, in the end, is my answer to the question every founder gets asked: why this?
The relationship I have with founderhood is not defined by title or aesthetics, but increasingly by my desire for ownership, agency and legacy.
Notes

What is ownership: I define ownership as not just share in the company stock, but control over the outcome (ownership over a project, ownership over a process, ownership over people). Ownership is the point at which “someone should fix this” quietly becomes “I will.”

What is agency: I think of it as a deep trust for your capacity to learn, adapt and figure things out, even if you do not know how to do something yet. Dr. Shadé Zahrai refers to this as a “belief” that you have the skills, capability, and capacity to achieve what you want. It is essentially a deep trust in your own capability. When you operate with a strong sense of agency, you believe that even if you do not know how to do something yet, you will persevere and succeed. Most of the founders have this in bucketloads.

What is legacy: I define legacy as leaving an impact on people, places and ecosystems, because of something you’ve built. Legacy can be visible in a company, a product, an institution, but it can also be embedded in the people who learned from it, the standards it changed or the possibilities it made easier for someone else to imagine. This is where founderhood starts to overlap with purpose.

essays.title: Velocity > Speed
essays.teaser: “Move fast and break things” is passé. In a world where everyone can build faster, speed is no longer the advantage it once was. The founders who win won't just move fast – they'll move with velocity: speed with direction.
essays.dek: “Move fast and break things” is passé. In a world where everyone can build faster, speed is no longer the advantage it once was.

body.text: In the past, Silicon Valley was built on one directive: move fast and break things. During the dot-com bubble, that instruction was radical because speed itself was the scarce resource — engineering teams were expensive, code took months to ship, teams took quarters to hire, distribution channels took years to build. Whoever moved fastest, least tied to tradition or convention, usually won.
Speed Got Cheap

That advantage is almost completely gone. AI has made speed cheap. What took a dot-com engineer six months now takes an AI-assisted founder a weekend, or even less for a 10x developer. Every founder has access to the same instant infrastructure, the same code-generation tools, the same distribution channels. When everyone can move fast, speed alone stops being the edge.

So what replaces it? Velocity — speed with direction. A company sprinting in the wrong direction just reaches the wrong destination sooner, and AI has only raised the speed at which founders can make expensive mistakes.

Velocity = speed × direction. When speed multiplies for free, direction becomes the only variable that still separates the founders who compound from the founders who just move.
Direction Is a Question of Purpose

Direction is really a question of purpose – not “how fast can we ship” but “why are we building this, and for whom.” That question used to get answered implicitly, over the months of a slower build cycle. AI removed that forced pause. Now founders have to build the pause back in deliberately with “intention”, otherwise they will ship their way into the wrong company faster than ever.
Time Is Relative

This is also a question of time horizon. Time is relative: an hour spent building the wrong thing costs a founder more than a week spent clarifying the right one. Founders building for a decade and founders building for a fundraising cycle should not be making the same trade-offs, but at AI speed, it is easy to let the calendar make that decision instead of making it on purpose. Time is cheap to spend now. Making it count is not automatic.

That said, Founder time remains a scarce resource. Yet it is precisely the resource required (ideally in abundance) to keep a company's strategy on course. Founders are often in constant motion — squeezing in one more meeting, one more client pitch, or one more investor conversation. It's difficult for them to give their undivided attention to asking or thinking about where the company is going, and how it is currently moving.
That is the pause or intervention Eklipse exists to force. Three focused, one-month cycles — clarity × alignment × execution = strategic velocity.
Strategic Leverage

The choice to dedicate time to collectively (or non-collectively) defining the future direction of a company is what separates founders who optimize for speed — more meetings, more hires, more launches, more fundraising — from founders who optimize for velocity: fewer, clearer decisions that compound with the right directive or guidance. Strategic leverage comes from exactly that gap: generating disproportionately greater outcomes from the same founder time and attention.

Time has always been a finite resource, and every founder still has the same allocation of it. What has changed is that AI made the wrong use of that resource amplified. The founders who win this decade will not be the ones who build fastest. They will be the ones who knew, before they started building, exactly what direction was worth that speed, and how to recruit people who are rowing in the same direction.

essays.title: What is an Eklipse?
essays.teaser: Every company navigates through constant shifts in its market, technology, and macro environment. An Eklipse is the recurring moment of alignment — where a company steps back, refocuses, and re-emerges with clarity on who it is, how it communicates, and how it moves forward.
essays.dek: Every company navigates through constant shifts in its market, technology, and macro environment. An Eklipse is the recurring moment of alignment.

body.text: Companies don't become misaligned once; they repeatedly drift out of alignment as their environment changes. An “Eklipse” is one of these moments of misalignment and realignment. Its magnitude depends on how much the company or its environment has changed. Sometimes an Eklipse is small, requiring only incremental adjustments. Other times, the gap is substantial, demanding a fundamental shift in strategy, structures, capabilities or overall direction.
Every Company Goes Through Eklipses

Companies don't always grow linearly: find product-market fit, raise capital, hire a team, scale. In reality, companies orbit through constant shifts in their markets, technologies, teams and macro environments. The company you built for one moment will not necessarily be the company you need for the next.

Over time, small inconsistencies begin to appear. The founder's vision evolves faster than the company narrative. The product changes while the positioning stays the same. New people join with different interpretations of the strategy. What the company says, what it believes and what it actually does slowly drift apart.
We call the moment when a company steps back, refocuses and brings those pieces back into alignment an Eklipse.
Eklipses Come in Different Magnitudes

Not every Eklipse is a transformation. Most are partial. Companies naturally go through smaller Eklipses as they evolve: refreshing a narrative after learning more about customers, reconsidering priorities after a new competitor emerges, or clarifying responsibilities as a team grows. These are periodic corrections that keep identity, narrative and execution moving together.

But sometimes the underlying change is much larger. A company pivots its business model. A new funding round changes its ambitions. A new CEO takes over. The company enters a different market, launches a major product or fundamentally changes how it competes. At these inflection points, the old system may no longer adequately describe the new company. Complexity increases precisely when strategic coherence matters most.

These moments create something closer to a total Eklipse: a deeper realignment across three layers — Strategic Identity, Strategic Narrative and Strategic Activation. The company must know who it is, articulate who it is, and then ensure its decisions and actions reflect that new reality.
Some Eklipses Happen Naturally

Good companies perform many of these corrections themselves. Founders rethink strategy. Leadership teams rewrite positioning and trickle it down to the rest of the teams. Boards pressure-test priorities and guide the C-suite in implementing new blueprints. Teams adapt. But there is a point where being inside the system makes the system difficult to see.

At major inflection points, founders are simultaneously making decisions, communicating those decisions and managing their consequences. Different stakeholders carry different pieces of context. What feels obvious to the founder may be ambiguous to everyone else. Strategic leverage begins to diminish as complexity increases. That is when an outside perspective can become useful — not to replace founder judgment, but to help structure it.
From Ambiguity to Velocity

A structured Eklipse begins with an inflection point and a diagnosis: where has strategic coherence broken? From there, founder vision is translated into strategic choices, narrative, priorities and stakeholder alignment.

The process moves through three one-month cycles: Identity establishes who the company is; Narrative determines how that identity is communicated; and Activation translates it into an execution roadmap. The aim is not simply to produce three documents. It is to create a system in which those choices propagate through the organization, so fewer decisions need to continuously return to the founder.

The result is strategic leverage — and ultimately, greater organizational velocity. That reflects the broader principle behind an Eklipse: clarity, alignment and execution multiply the impact of the resources a company already has. Every company will undergo different rounds of change throughout its lifetime. The key question is whether it periodically realigns itself with what it has become? And how fast it can achieve that realignment.
An “Eklipse” is a natural part of company-building, but its magnitude depends on how much a founder is willing and able to change a company’s trajectory.
